idle: Minus four on the glass. In 1974 it was minus six.
Albert would have said the boards need paint. He'd have been right.
That's eight of mine and five of his.
good_ice: Oh, that's a dinner plate. Just like opening night.
First lap on fresh ice. There's nothing like it, dear.
bad_ice: Bumpy as the Church Street sidewalk.
I'll take it slow. Slower. Albert's laps can wait.
wet_ice: Slush. I didn't wait fifty-two years to wade.
My skates are wet through. Albert would have said something.
cold: I've got two scarves and a hot water bottle in my purse. Don't tell anyone.
Colder than the switchboard room, and that's saying something.
hungry: It's nearly 2:15. Is the hot chocolate on?
long_line: A queue! Well. I've waited longer for worse.
greet_owner: There's the owner. Take my arm.
Hello, dear. It's {ice_word} today, but I've seen worse.
leaving_happy: Twelve for me and twelve for Albert. Same time next week.
leaving_angry: I've been coming since 1974, dear. I'd like to keep coming. Make it easy for me.

public_skate: Not on your phone in the lane, young man.
Is that the Skaters' Waltz? No. Pity.
figure_practice: I come early for the end of practice. That little Thibodeau girl can fly.
senior_hockey: Kessler won the opener in 1974, you know. I'm still cross.

first.say: (She takes your arm before you offer it.) You must be the new owner. Irene Dubois. I was here opening night, 2 November 1974. It was minus six and the ice was harder than a church pew.

options.text: Let me walk you to the bench.
Sorry, I'm in a bit of a rush.

first_since.say: Except two winters. My hip, and then Albert's. He's gone now, so I skate his laps too. Twelve for me, twelve for him. It keeps me honest.

first_arm.say: Oh, you've got manners. That was rarer in 1974 than you'd think. Albert walked me to the bench once and then went for a hot dog.

options.text: I'm sorry, Irene. I'll do better.

say: It's minus four on the glass, dear. In 1974 it was minus six. We were tougher then, and colder.
I've done eight of mine and five of Albert's. He's slower than he used to be.

albert_lap_greet.say: There's my partner. One of Albert's laps is yours, if you want it. He won't mind. He's not using it.

say: There you are. Take my arm. No, the other one. That one's for Albert.
Hello, dear. I saved you a spot on the bench. It's cold, but it's yours.
Hello, dear. It's {time}, so I've got until hot chocolate.
Sit down a minute. The bench is cold but the company isn't.

options.text: What did you do before you retired?
What do you love about public skate?
Who else do you see here?
How does the rink compare to 1974?

job.say: I ran the switchboard at the telephone exchange for thirty-one years. I knew everyone's business and I told nobody. Mostly nobody.

events.say: Friday public skate, the end of figure practice if I'm early, and the Lumber Kings when Doreen drags me. But the waltz is the thing. A rink is a ballroom that's honest about the floor.

albert.say: He skated like a man pushing a lawnmower, and he held my hand every lap for forty years. I do his laps now. It's not sad, dear. It's arithmetic.

options.text: Could I skate one of his laps with you sometime?

do.note: Irene Dubois has offered you one of Albert's laps at public skate.

albert_yes.say: Oh. Yes. He'd like that. He'd say you're leaning too far forward, but he'd like it.

gossip.say: Jess brings her little one on Fridays. Birdie and I waltz at two miles an hour and she falls at every bar line. And Doreen thinks her organ hung the moon. It did, in 1979.

rink.say: In 1974 the paint was new and the ice was a dinner plate. Now the paint's older than most of the skaters and the ice is {ice_word}.

rink_better.say: It's the best it's been since Albert complained about it. That's a compliment, dear. He complained about everything good.

say: Off you go. I've got Albert's laps to do.
Same time next week, dear. I'm not done.
